readings.title: The entrance that a map forgot
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A town museum advertised itself as accessible because a ramp had been built at a side door. Visitors arriving by bus, however, followed the main map to a staircase. Some turned back before discovering the ramp. Staff invited wheelchair users and parents with pushchairs to travel from the bus stop to the entrance. The exercise revealed missing signs at two corners. The museum updated its map and placed directions where visitors actually made choices. The ramp had already removed a physical barrier; the new information made that improvement usable.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：篇章结构与信息判断

readings.title: A bus shelter tested in the rain
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: Designers showed residents a drawing of a new bus shelter. It looked attractive, but an older passenger asked where rain would fall when the wind blew from the west. The team built a simple full-size model and observed it on a wet afternoon. Water reached part of the bench, and the route display was hard to read from a seated position. The design was adjusted before permanent construction. Testing the model took extra time, but changing it was cheaper than rebuilding the finished shelter. Residents felt their practical experience had shaped the result.

readings.title: When a longer route became preferable
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A journey-planning app usually recommended the fastest walk between the station and hospital. That route included a steep hill. After receiving comments, the developers added information about slopes, steps and places to rest. Users could choose a gentler route that took seven minutes longer. The team did not label either route as best for everyone. A visitor carrying luggage might value fewer steps, while someone in a hurry might choose the shorter path. Showing the trade-off helped people make decisions according to their needs instead of relying on one hidden definition of convenience.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：篇章结构与信息判断

readings.title: A crossing with enough time
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: Near a community clinic, pedestrians had only a short period to cross a wide street. Complaints focused on slow walkers feeling rushed. Engineers first measured the average crossing speed, but an average concealed the experience of those who needed longer. They observed journeys by older residents and people using walking aids. The signal was then adjusted at busy clinic times. Traffic queues grew slightly, so the town monitored both waiting times and pedestrian comfort. The project treated safe access as an important purpose of the street, alongside moving vehicles efficiently.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A route that is convenient for one person may be difficult for another. Steps, steep slopes and a lack of resting places can all affect a journey. Providing this information allows travellers to make their own choices. Good public services do not assume that every user moves at the same speed or has the same priorities. They make differences visible and offer practical alternatives.
knowledgePoints: 英译汉：语义准确与中文表达
translation.explanation: 注意that引导的定语从句、动名词主语及priorities在语境中的含义。
translation.referenceAnswer: 对一个人来说方便的路线，对另一个人却可能很困难。台阶、陡坡以及缺少休息地点都可能影响行程。提供这些信息可以让出行者自己作出选择。良好的公共服务不会假定所有使用者都以同样的速度行动，或有同样的优先考虑。它们让差异清楚可见，并提供切实可行的替代方案。

writing.stem: Write 100–150 words in English to a town transport office. Describe one difficulty faced by passengers with limited mobility, suggest an improvement, and explain how passengers could help assess it.
knowledgePoints: 写作：任务完成、组织与语言
writing.explanation: 说明具体出行障碍、对应改善以及乘客参与评估的方式。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Transport Officer,
I would like to raise a difficulty at the bus stop outside the community clinic. The route display is positioned high above the bench, so passengers who need to remain seated cannot easily read it.
Could a second display be placed at a suitable height beside the seats? It should use clear lettering and include notices about temporary route changes. This would also help passengers carrying bags or travelling with children.
Before installing it permanently, the office could put up a temporary version for two weeks. Passengers could comment on its height, print size and visibility in different weather. Clinic volunteers might help collect these comments during busy hours. This small trial would give the office useful information before spending more money.
Yours faithfully,
A local passenger
